# Shaping the Table {#chp:structure}

::: epigraph
> Form ever follows function.
>
> ---Louis Sullivan, *The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered*
:::

A table is not only a grid of values. It has a shape: a few columns that belong
together under a shared heading, rows that form families, a child row that hangs
off its parent, and a column or two that exists only to feed the others. This is
the chapter where you give your table that shape.

## Merging columns {#sec:merge}

Consider a row that reads "Age: 67 (100%)". The number and the percentage belong
together, so they should share a cell. `lt_merge()` does exactly that: the first
column you name receives the combined text, and a pattern says how to put the
pieces together. `{1}` is the first column, `{2}` the second, and so on.

```{r, child = ex('merge')}
```

By default, the source columns (all but the first) are hidden, since their
content now lives in the target. Set `hide = FALSE` if you want to keep them
visible.

Sometimes one of the pieces is missing, and the sentence should not be left
dangling with an empty parenthesis. Wrap the optional part in `<<` and `>>`, and
it vanishes whenever any value it refers to is missing. In the example above,
the `Tertiary` row has no confidence interval, so the whole `(lo, hi)` part is
dropped, while the rows that have one keep it. This is a small trick with a large
payoff in real reports, where missing pieces are common.

`lt_merge()` uses the displayed values. Format the source columns first with
`lt_format()`, as the example does, so that the merged text reads
`0.61 (0.40, 0.82)` and not the raw `0.6123 (0.401234, ...)`.

## Column spanners {#sec:spanner}

A spanner is a label that sits above a run of columns, telling the reader that
these columns are one family. Name it with a formula, `Label ~ col1 + col2`.
The columns must be next to each other, but you do not have to list them in
visual order: **lt** reorders them to match the body.

```{r, child = ex('spanner')}
```

If your columns already share a prefix, you may not need to name anything at
all. Calling `lt_spanner()` with no arguments looks for a common prefix before
the first `.` or `_` and groups the columns that share it, shortening each
column label to its suffix. In the example, `Sepal.Length` and `Sepal.Width`
collapse under a "Sepal" spanner, and their labels become "Length" and "Width".

## Moving and hiding columns {#sec:move-hide}

Your data frame has the column order it has, but the report should read
differently. `lt_move()` shuffles columns without touching the data. Name the
columns to move and say where to put them with `after`: a column name, a
position, or `NULL` for the very front.

`lt_hide()` is the quieter cousin. It removes columns from the table, but not
from the data behind it. That distinction matters: a hidden column still travels
with each row, so an interactive table can use it for a row's detail pane (see
@sec:detail). Hiding is therefore the right tool for "useful, but not on the
page".

```{r, child = ex('move-hide')}
```

Use `lt_hide()` when a value helps a reader but clutters the page. If you want a
column gone for good, drop it from the data frame before calling `lt()`.

## Row groups {#sec:group}

Tables are easier to scan when rows come in families. `lt_group()` partitions the
rows by the values of one or more columns, and removes those columns from the
body so that the group labels do the work instead.

By default, groups are drawn as **rowspan** cells that run down the left side,
which is compact and looks like the tables in many journals. But a long group
label does not fit in a narrow cell, so **lt** switches to full-width
**separator rows** on its own when a single text column has a label longer than
20 characters. You can force either style with `sep = TRUE` (separator rows) or
`sep = FALSE` (rowspan cells). Separator rows take only one grouping column, while
rowspan cells can nest several, one inside another.

```{r, child = ex('group')}
```

Groups are sorted by default, so that identical values sit together. If your
rows already come in the order you want, `sort = FALSE` keeps them as they are.

### Manual groups and their order {#sec:group-manual}

Sometimes no column tells the story. Maybe the first three rows are the
treatment arm because you know it from the study design, not because a column
says so. In that case, name the row ranges yourself: `"Label" = rows` makes a
group from a set of row numbers.

The same trick reorders groups. Pass the group labels, unnamed, to a later
`lt_group()` call, and those groups move to the front in the order you list them.

```{r, child = ex('group-manual')}
```

## Indentation {#sec:indent}

Hierarchies such as adverse events, where "Cardiac" contains "Tachycardia", read
best when the children are indented under their parent. `lt_indent()` nudges the
first column of the chosen rows to the right, one `level` per step. Call it once
for the parents and again for the children, with a deeper level.

```{r, child = ex('indent')}
```

Indentation is about looks; it does not change which rows belong to which parent.
If you also want interactive sorting to keep each child with its parent, see
@sec:structure.
